rationale: The report that Nicanor and his army have fallen refers to the preceding account of Nicanor's death and the destruction of his fleeing force.
The renewed dispatch of Bacchides and Alcimus repeats the king's earlier joint commission of these two men against Judah.
The men's fear at their numerical disadvantage recalls the earlier objection that Judas's few men could not face a multitude; the earlier speech insisted that strength comes from Heaven.
The survivors' refusal to fight because they are few repeats the numerical objection Judas previously answered by distinguishing heavenly strength from army size.
Judas's resolve to die courageously for his brothers continues his earlier preference for death in battle over witnessing the nation's suffering.

Judas's men sounding trumpets against their adversaries corresponds to the prescribed trumpet signal in defensive war; the subsequent defeat is not represented as a fulfilment of the law's promise of deliverance.
Judas's death ends the military leadership assigned to him by Mattathias, who had designated him the brothers' army commander.
Judas is buried in the ancestral tomb at Modein, the place where the book previously reports Mattathias's burial.
Jonathan is later brought to the same family burial place at Modein, where Simon constructs the memorial for his parents and brothers.
All Israel's great lament for Judas repeats the national lament already reported at Mattathias's burial, marking the loss of successive leaders.
The lament asking how the mighty one has fallen recalls the repeated refrain in David's lament over Saul and Jonathan; Judas is the fallen leader here, not either figure in that earlier lament.
The lawless resurgence after Judas's death reverses the earlier situation in which Judas's campaign prevented the deserters associated with Alcimus from moving through the country.
Bacchides's appointment of ungodly rulers renews his earlier arrangement placing the country under Alcimus and the men who afflicted Israel.
The persecution of Judas's friends implements the earlier request that the king punish Judas and everyone helping him, the request that led to Bacchides's commission.
The reference to the absence of a prophet accords with the earlier decision to reserve the altar stones until a prophet should come to answer about them.
The later settlement of Simon's leadership likewise waits for a faithful prophet to arise, continuing the book's explicit awareness of absent prophetic arbitration.
The need for a successor who will go out and come in before Israel resembles Moses' request for a leader who will go out and come in before the congregation after him.
The people's choice of Jonathan to lead and fight their war is repeated when they later acclaim Simon as successor to Judas and Jonathan and ask him to fight their war.
The later public inscription summarizes the leadership begun here by recalling that Jonathan gathered the nation and became its high priest.
Jonathan's company escaping pursuit into the wilderness repeats the earlier withdrawal of persecuted covenant observers and the royal pursuit that followed them.
Bacchides's Sabbath pursuit recalls the earlier Sabbath attack on wilderness fugitives and the community's subsequent decision to defend itself on that day.
Jonathan's appeal to the Nabateans as friends has a precedent in the earlier peaceful reception that they gave him and Judas during the Gilead expedition.
The John seized here is identified in the surrounding account as Jonathan and Simon's brother, corresponding to the John listed among Mattathias's sons.
Jonathan and Simon's remembrance of their brother's blood explains their ambush as revenge for the seizure of John and the entrusted property earlier in this episode.

The wedding turning to mourning and its music to lament closely recalls the prophetic language of festivals becoming mourning and songs becoming lamentation; no identification of the wedding as Amos's predicted event is asserted.
The declaration that the brothers have avenged their brother's blood explicitly closes the account that began with John's seizure while transporting their belongings.
The renewed attack on the Sabbath supplies the precise defensive situation for which Mattathias's company had resolved to fight rather than remain unresisting.
Jonathan's summons to fight for their lives, in the Sabbath setting of the preceding verse, follows the earlier decision to defend their lives when attacked on the Sabbath.
Jonathan's description of battle before and behind his men resembles Judah's encirclement before and behind in Chronicles, where the trapped defenders also cry to God; these are separate battles.
Jonathan's appeal to cry to Heaven for rescue continues the earlier assembly's cry to Heaven and confession that Israel could not stand without divine help.
The strongholds Bacchides builds here are explicitly recalled when their foreign occupants later abandon them following Jonathan's rise in authority.
The hostile garrisons installed in Bacchides's strongholds later flee and return to their own lands, reversing this deployment against Israel.
Bacchides's reinforcement of Beth-zur prepares the later account of Simon expelling its occupants and replacing them with his own garrison.
The provisioned citadel later suffers fatal shortage under blockade and surrenders to Simon, reversing its secure military position here.
The hostages detained in Jerusalem's citadel are the captives whom Demetrius later orders released to Jonathan and whom Jonathan restores to their parents.

Alcimus's attack on the holy precincts contrasts with the earlier expectation that his Aaronic priesthood meant he would do no wrong, an expectation already broken by his violence against those seeking peace.
The lawless men's proposal to bring Bacchides against Jonathan ends with Bacchides's failed expedition and his killing many of the very advisers who summoned him.
The failure of secret plans to seize Jonathan because they become known recalls Judas's discovery of Nicanor's deceptive attempt to seize him.
Bacchides's investment in siege engines at Beth-basi is overturned when Simon burns the engines and the failed expedition turns Bacchides against its instigators.
Simon's destruction of the siege engines directly defeats the equipment Bacchides had constructed for the prolonged attack on Beth-basi.
Bacchides turns against the lawless advisers whose promise of an easy capture had drawn him back into the country.
Bacchides's oath not to harm Jonathan is followed by release and withdrawal, contrasting with the earlier peaceful oath to the Hasideans that was followed by their killing.
The return of captives and final withdrawal fulfil the two concrete results of Jonathan's peace negotiation: release of captives and cessation of hostility.
Jonathan's settled rule, peace, and removal of the ungodly anticipate the later description of Simon's peaceful rule and removal of lawless people.
The later account identifies the young Antiochus as Alexander's son and proposed successor; this preserves the distinction between Alexander and the Antiochus named here as his father.
Demetrius's initial approach to Jonathan is followed by his complaint that Alexander has gained Jewish support first and by his decision to offer further honours and gifts.
Demetrius hopes to prevent Jonathan's alliance with Alexander, but the narrative later records rejection of his promises and lasting alliance with Alexander.
Demetrius's acknowledgment of injuries to Jonathan's family and nation recalls his earlier dispatch of Bacchides and Alcimus to exact vengeance in Israel.
The order to hand over the citadel's hostages addresses the earlier seizure of the country leaders' sons by Bacchides.
Jonathan's restoration of the hostages to their parents reverses their detention in the citadel after Bacchides took the leaders' sons.
Jonathan's move to Jerusalem and renewal of the city follow his earlier settlement and judicial leadership at Michmash, marking the expansion of his governing position.
The later deliberation to raise Jerusalem's walls and repair a fallen section continues the fortification work Jonathan commissions here.
The flight from the strongholds explicitly reverses Bacchides's earlier building and garrisoning of those places against Israel.
The foreign occupants' abandonment of their posts dismantles the network of hostile garrisons that Bacchides had installed in Judea.
Beth-zur's survival as a refuge for those who abandoned the law explains the later need for Simon to besiege it and expel its occupants.
Alexander's response is explicitly prompted by the promises Demetrius has sent Jonathan, including military authority and release of hostages.
Alexander's recognition of Jonathan's strength has a concrete narrative precedent in the resistance to Bacchides that forced a negotiated withdrawal and release of captives.
The high priesthood and royal honours first conferred by Alexander are subsequently confirmed to Jonathan by Demetrius.
The young Antiochus later confirms Jonathan's high priesthood and royal friendship and renews permission to wear purple, continuing the honours granted here.

The seventh-month Festival of Booths at which Jonathan dons the holy robe corresponds to the law's seventh-month Feast of Tents; the law supplies the festival calendar, not authorization for Alexander's priestly appointment.
Demetrius's complaint that Alexander anticipated him reverses his own earlier intention to secure Jonathan's agreement before Alexander could do so.
The new offer of honours and gifts fails to gain Jonathan's support because the people distrust Demetrius and choose Alexander's alliance.
The later letter from Demetrius son of Demetrius again remits dues, salt revenues, and crown payments, repeating the kinds of concessions offered by his father here without equating the two kings.

The later royal letter also connects the three districts added from Samaria with remission of royal dues on land produce and fruit trees; its named districts should not erase this letter's mention of Galilee.
The proposal to exempt Jerusalem from tithes and dues is comparable to the later king's grant of tithes and dues, although the letters belong to different Demetrius reigns.

The father's proposed surrender of the citadel contrasts with Jonathan's later need to ask his son Demetrius to remove its hostile occupants; the earlier offer was not accepted as an achieved transfer.

The proposed free release of Jewish captives extends the kind of concrete release Jonathan had already obtained from Bacchides through negotiation; the royal proposal is not presented as accomplished.
The proposed attachment of three Samaritan districts to Judea is followed by the later Demetrius's confirmation naming Aphairema, Lydda, and Rathamin.
The promise of royal funding for sanctuary restoration belongs to the concessions that Jonathan and the people explicitly decline to believe or accept.

Demetrius offers to fund the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, the specific project Jonathan has already begun, making the promise a response to an existing need rather than a report of completed payment.
The refusal to trust Demetrius's promises is illuminated by the earlier violated oath and killings under the agents he commissioned against Israel.
The statement that Jonathan remained Alexander's ally all his days reaches its narrative limit when Alexander is killed; it is not extended to Jonathan's later relations with other rulers.
The death of this Demetrius prepares for the later arrival of Demetrius son of Demetrius, distinguishing father from son without supplying unsourced regnal numbers.
Alexander's claim to have defeated Demetrius and gained the kingdom retells the battle and Demetrius's death just narrated, now as the basis for his appeal to Ptolemy.
The envoy's account of Demetrius and his force being crushed recapitulates the narrated victory rather than introducing a second battle.
Alexander's proposed marriage alliance with Ptolemy is later undone when Ptolemy removes his daughter and gives her to Alexander's rival Demetrius.
Ptolemy's promise to meet Alexander at Ptolemais and establish the marriage is carried out by his arrival with Cleopatra and the wedding there.
Cleopatra's arrival for marriage to Alexander supplies the prior relationship that Ptolemy later breaks by giving his daughter to Demetrius.
The marriage to Ptolemy's daughter explains why Alexander later orders the cities to welcome Ptolemy as his father-in-law.
Jonathan's presentation of gifts and favourable reception at Ptolemais is repeated under Demetrius, who similarly honours him despite accusations.
The unsuccessful accusations by lawless Israelites against Jonathan recur at his later royal audience, when his position and honours are again confirmed.
The public clothing of Jonathan in purple gives visible expression to the royal honour already signified when Alexander sent him a purple robe with his appointment.
The proclamation barring petitions against Jonathan answers the lawless men's attempt to petition the king against him.
Demetrius later confirms Jonathan's prior honours and rank among the First Friends, the rank Alexander grants here.
The son of Demetrius introduced as a claimant here subsequently becomes king after the deaths of Alexander and Ptolemy.
Apollonius is appointed by the Demetrius newly introduced as the son of the earlier king, identifying the political side he serves without equating him with other men named Apollonius.
Apollonius boasts that Jonathan cannot stand against cavalry in the plain, but Jonathan's men hold firm until the horses tire and the cavalry scatters.
Simon's arrival to help Jonathan accords with Mattathias's earlier instruction that the brothers listen to Simon as their counsellor; the target does not specify this battle.
Joppa's earlier role as a stronghold of Demetrius's commander explains the later concern that it might again be handed to Demetrius's men and Simon's placement of a guarding garrison.
Jonathan's acquisition of Joppa precedes the later account of Simon securing it as the nation's harbour; the stages are not collapsed into one capture.
Apollonius deliberately draws the battle into the plain because he trusts his cavalry, but the subsequent account makes the horses' exhaustion decisive in his defeat.
The defenders' endurance and the horses' exhaustion answer Apollonius's challenge that they could not stand before his cavalry on the plain.
The flight into Beth-dagon leads to the burned shrine and dead that are later shown to Ptolemy as evidence against Jonathan.
The burning of Azotus and Dagon's temple is explicitly recalled when the inhabitants show Ptolemy the ruins and accuse Jonathan.

Both narratives portray humiliation of Dagon's cult in its sanctuary, here by Jonathan's burning and there by the idol falling before the ark; Azotus and Ashdod are kept as the texts name them, and identity of the buildings is not asserted.
The dead by sword and fire are recalled in the bodies and burned victims displayed along Ptolemy's route; the later account does not independently repeat the numerical total.
Ascalon's honourable reception of Jonathan is explicitly repeated during his later journey with the Syrian forces allied to him.
Alexander's further honour after the campaign builds upon his earlier appointment of Jonathan as high priest and king's Friend.
The young Antiochus later authorizes Jonathan to wear the golden clasp, continuing a distinction first bestowed here by Alexander.
Ptolemy's concealed attempt to seize Alexander's kingdom reverses the friendship and marriage alliance that had linked the two kings.
Alexander's instruction to welcome Ptolemy as his father-in-law depends on the earlier wedding of Alexander and Ptolemy's daughter Cleopatra.
Ptolemy's garrisons in the cities are later destroyed after his death, marking the collapse of the occupation he establishes during his peaceful-looking entry.
The ruined Dagon temple, burned towns, and bodies shown to Ptolemy explicitly recall Jonathan's defeat of Apollonius and burning of the refuge at Azotus.
The accusations against Jonathan concern the burning and casualties already narrated, although Ptolemy's silence supplies no verdict endorsing them.
Jonathan can receive Ptolemy at Joppa after having gained control of that city in the campaign against Apollonius.
Ptolemy now offers Demetrius the daughter previously given to Alexander, deliberately undoing the marriage alliance formed at Ptolemais.

The allegation that Alexander sought Ptolemy's life is framed by the narrator's prior statement that Ptolemy intended to obtain Alexander's kingdom deceitfully; the allegation is not independently established.
The narrator's explanation that Ptolemy accused Alexander because he wanted the kingdom repeats the motive disclosed before Ptolemy's peaceful-looking journey.
Ptolemy's transfer of his daughter to Demetrius breaks the marriage with Alexander celebrated in the earlier account.
Ptolemy's wearing the diadems of Egypt and Asia visibly expresses his initial plan to add Alexander's kingdom to his own.
Alexander's death closes the period described by the statement that Jonathan and the people remained his allies all his days.
The destruction of Ptolemy's men after his death reverses his earlier stationing of garrisons in the cities he entered.
Demetrius's accession completes the movement begun when Demetrius son of Demetrius returned from Crete to claim his fathers' land.
Jonathan's siege engines against Jerusalem's citadel renew the earlier effort of Judas to remove the hostile garrison by siege.
Lawless men reporting Jonathan's siege to the king repeat the earlier appeal by the citadel's allies for royal intervention against Judas's siege.
Jonathan again brings rich gifts to a royal meeting at Ptolemais and finds favour, as he had done before Alexander and Ptolemy.
The lawless men's petitions against Jonathan repeat the earlier unsuccessful accusations presented at his royal reception in Ptolemais.
The statement that the king honours Jonathan as earlier rulers had done refers back to Alexander's public investiture and promotion of him.
Demetrius confirms the high priesthood that Alexander had previously granted Jonathan.
Jonathan's confirmation among the First Friends maintains the distinguished rank previously granted by Alexander.
Jonathan's request for tax exemption in Judea and the three districts seeks benefits of the kind earlier proposed by Demetrius's father; the two Demetrius kings remain distinct.
The confirmation names the three districts and replaces royal agricultural dues, developing the same territorial and fiscal subjects addressed in the previous Demetrius's rejected offer.
The remission of tithes, dues, salt revenues, and crown payments repeats the principal tax categories in the earlier king's offer, without implying that the earlier proposal was accepted.
The order to display the royal letter on the holy mountain resembles the later instruction to display the national settlement on bronze within the holy enclosure and preserve copies in the treasury.
Demetrius's dismissal of his inherited forces explains why those same dismissed forces later rally to the young Antiochus and defeat him.
Tryphon's approach to the guardian of Alexander's young son leads to his return with the boy Antiochus, who is then crowned.
Tryphon's stated project of placing Alexander's son on his father's throne is later exposed as temporary when he seeks the diadem for himself and plots against Antiochus.
Jonathan's complaint that the citadel's occupants fight Israel repeats the earlier characterization of that garrison as continually harming Israel and supporting the nations.
Demetrius's assurance of benefit and honour is contradicted by the narrator's later report that he proved false to his promises and oppressed Jonathan.
Demetrius's request for Jewish troops because his forces have revolted follows his own dismissal of the inherited army and its resulting hostility.
Jonathan's dispatch of three thousand men supplies the concrete goodwill that the later judgment says Demetrius failed to repay.
The Jews' saving of Demetrius makes the later report of his failure to repay their goodwill a pointed indictment of ingratitude.
The honour shown to the returning Jewish force is followed by Demetrius's estrangement and oppression of Jonathan, reversing the favourable reception earned by the rescue.
The narrator's charge of falsehood and ingratitude refers to Demetrius's promises of help and honour and Jonathan's answering gift of troops.
Tryphon's return with the crowned boy realizes his earlier effort to obtain Alexander's son Antiochus from his guardian.
The troops who rally against Demetrius are expressly the forces he dismissed earlier, turning his military policy into the cause of his defeat.
The young Antiochus renews Jonathan's high priesthood and royal friendship, honours first granted here by his father Alexander.
Permission to wear the golden clasp continues the distinction that Alexander had previously sent Jonathan after the Azotus campaign.
Simon's coastal command is followed by his movement through Ascalon and his securing Joppa against transfer to Demetrius's men.
Ascalon's honourable welcome repeats its reception of Jonathan after his earlier victory at Azotus.
Demetrius's commanders who arrive to displace Jonathan return in the following chapter with a larger force, continuing the same opposition.
Simon's siege addresses the continued hostile refuge at Beth-zur that remained after the other foreign garrisons fled.
The later inscription recalls Simon's replacement of the hostile establishment at Beth-zur with a Jewish garrison, the change effected here.

The combination of a frontal force and a hidden force behind Jonathan's army resembles Jeroboam's two-sided attack on Judah; both narratives place prayer within the ensuing crisis without equating the battles.
Jonathan's abandonment by nearly all his men recalls the earlier desertion of Judas before his final battle; the two narratives then give different outcomes for the leaders who remain.
Jonathan's torn garments, earth on his head, and prayer repeat the penitential gestures and appeal for heavenly help used by Judas's assembly before battle.
The return of those who fled explicitly reverses the army's abandonment of Jonathan, allowing them to share the pursuit after his counterattack.
Jonathan's mission to renew Roman friendship continues the original embassy sent by Judas to establish that alliance.
The later Spartan letter records reception of Jonathan's named envoys and their mission to renew friendship, corresponding to his initiative here.
The envoys' entry into the Roman council chamber and request to renew the former alliance repeat the setting and subject of Judas's original mission.

The Roman letters protecting the envoys' journey resemble the later letters to foreign authorities protecting Jewish interests; the later letters accompany Simon's embassy and are not treated as the same documents.
The Spartan reply later addresses the high priest, elders, priests, and people as brothers, matching the corporate parties and fraternal address in Jonathan's letter.
Jonathan explicitly points to the copy below; that copy names Areus and Onias and states the claimed brotherhood of Spartans and Jews.
The embedded letter supplies the declaration of kinship and shared interests that Jonathan describes Onias as having accepted; it does not independently narrate the envoy's reception.
Jonathan identifies the holy books as encouragement, while Romans likewise speaks of the encouragement of the Scriptures producing hope; the statements belong to distinct authors and circumstances.
The wish to renew friendship receives a documented response when Sparta records the mission of Numenius and Antipater to renew that friendship.
The letter's summary of surrounding wars has an immediate example in Demetrius's commanders attempting to remove Jonathan and fighting him in Galilee.
The claim of heavenly help and rescue has a concrete preceding example in Jonathan's prayer after his men fled and the subsequent reversal of the battle.
The later Spartan record repeats both envoys' names and fathers, Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, confirming the personnel of the renewal mission.
The Roman mission is expressly a renewal of the friendship first established through Judas's differently named envoys; the two embassies are distinguished.
The instruction that the envoys visit Sparta is reflected in Sparta's subsequent public record of their arrival and mission to renew friendship.
Jonathan's request for an answer is followed in the book by the Spartan letter reporting the reception of his envoys and preservation of their words.
The copied letter's address from Areus to Onias supplies the named royal and priestly correspondents invoked in Jonathan's introduction.

The earlier letter's claim of brotherhood continues in Sparta's later fraternal address to Simon and the Jewish people; that later address does not verify the claim of biological descent from Abraham.

The offer of shared property and mutual welfare explains why Jonathan characterizes the old letter as declaring alliance and friendship; it is diplomatic language, not a demonstrated transfer of ownership.
The return of Demetrius's commanders with a larger army resumes their previous attempt to remove Jonathan and their defeat in Galilee.
Jonathan's full-night readiness answers the spies' warning of a night attack and prompts the enemy's fearful withdrawal, although their fires delay discovery of that withdrawal.
The fires lit by the retreating enemy explain why Jonathan's men do not discover the withdrawal until morning, by which time pursuit cannot overtake them.
Simon's movement through Ascalon and Joppa exercises the coastal command previously assigned to him from the Ladder of Tyre to Egypt's borders.
The risk of Joppa passing to Demetrius's men recalls its earlier occupation by Apollonius's garrison before Jonathan gained control; Simon now secures it with a guard.
Jonathan's deliberations about Judean strongholds are continued under Simon, who rebuilds and provisions the strongholds with walls, towers, gates, and bars.
The planned isolation of the citadel so that its occupants cannot buy or sell leads to the later account of hunger under blockade and surrender to Simon.
The repair of Jerusalem's fallen wall continues the rebuilding and fortification Jonathan began after settling in the city.
Simon's fortification of Adida prepares the place where he later encamps facing Tryphon's army in the plain.
Tryphon's intention to seize the diadem and act against Antiochus is realized when he kills the young king and reigns in his place.
Tryphon's fear that Jonathan will defend Antiochus is understandable in light of Antiochus's confirmation of Jonathan's offices and his appointment of Simon to a command.
Tryphon's fear of Jonathan's large force explains his effort to dismiss that force before seizing Jonathan inside Ptolemais.
Tryphon's honourable reception conceals an intended seizure, resembling Nicanor's peaceful reception of Judas while enemies waited to seize him; Judas detected that earlier deception.
Tryphon promises to hand over Ptolemais, but its people instead close the gates and seize Jonathan when he enters, reversing the promised transfer of control.

Jonathan's trust in a peaceful assurance precedes seizure and slaughter, recalling the Hasideans' earlier trust in an oath that was followed by their killing; the two victims and agents remain distinct.
The two thousand left in Galilee explain the remaining company that Tryphon tries to destroy after Jonathan's capture and that returns safely to Judea.
Jonathan's capture at Ptolemais continues with his detention by Tryphon and the unsuccessful ransom negotiation, showing that capture did not itself constitute his death.

relationship: same-chapter pursuit of the detached force
rationale: Tryphon's force sent into Galilee targets the men Jonathan had left there when he went to Ptolemais with the smaller escort.
The men's report that Jonathan has perished must be distinguished from the subsequent narrative: he is still under guard, is the subject of ransom demands, and is killed later at Bascama.
Israel's mourning at the report of Jonathan's loss precedes the later mourning when Simon retrieves his bones after his actual killing; the two scenes are not collapsed chronologically.
The nations' plan to remove Israel's memory recalls the psalm's conspiracy to destroy Israel as a nation so its name is remembered no more, using the supplied Greek-numbered Psalm 82.
The enemies' assertion that Israel has no ruler is answered when Simon gathers the frightened people and is acclaimed their leader in place of Judas and Jonathan.
